claim: Hippocampal place cells fire at different rates when a rodent runs through a given location on its way to different destinations.
source: Hippocampal place cells fire at different rates when a rodent runs through a given location on its way to different destinations.
evidence: This is a well-established finding cited from prior literature and forms the basis for the current study.

claim: Lister Hooded rats (n = 8) were trained to navigate from a start box to three goal locations via four partially overlapping routes.
source: Lister Hooded rats (n = 8) were trained to navigate from a start box to three goal locations via four partially overlapping routes.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and subject details.

claim: Two of the four routes led to the same goal location.
source: Two of these led to the same goal location.
evidence: This is a key feature of the experimental design described in the abstract.

claim: 95.8% of cells that fired on the two routes to the same goal showed route-dependent firing.
source: Of the cells that fired on these two routes, 95.8% showed route-dependent firing (firing on only one route), whereas only two cells (4.2%) showed goal-dependent firing (firing similarly on both routes).
evidence: This is a primary quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: Only 4.2% of cells (two cells) showed goal-dependent firing on the two routes to the same goal.
source: Of the cells that fired on these two routes, 95.8% showed route-dependent firing (firing on only one route), whereas only two cells (4.2%) showed goal-dependent firing (firing similarly on both routes).
evidence: This is a primary quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: Route-dependent place cells over-represented the less discriminable routes.
source: In addition, route-dependent place cells over-represented the less discriminable routes, and place cells in general over-represented the start location.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of place cell distribution.

claim: Place cells in general over-represented the start location.
source: In addition, route-dependent place cells over-represented the less discriminable routes, and place cells in general over-represented the start location.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of place cell distribution.

claim: Place cell firing on overlapping routes reflects the animal's route, not its goals.
source: These results indicate that place cell firing on overlapping routes reflects the animal's route, not its goals, and that this firing may aid spatial discrimination.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Place cell firing may aid spatial discrimination.
source: These results indicate that place cell firing on overlapping routes reflects the animal's route, not its goals, and that this firing may aid spatial discrimination.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: The hippocampus contains a neural representation of space, a 'cognitive map' (Tolman, 1948), that encodes locations via the spatial receptive fields of place cells (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; O'Keefe, 1999).
source: A long-standing view of the hippocampus is that it contains a neural representation of space, a 'cognitive map' (Tolman, 1948), that encodes locations via the spatial receptive fields of place cells (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; O'Keefe, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: When a rat repeatedly traverses the same location on its way to different destinations, the place fields of hippocampal place cells are strongly modulated by where the animal is going or where it has come from (Wood et al., 2000; Frank et al., 2000; Ferbinteanu and Shapiro, 2003; Bower et al., 2005; Ainge et al., 2007; Ji and Wilson, 2008; Pastalkova et al., 2008; Ferbinteanu et al., 2011; Allen et al., 2012; Catanese et al., 2014; Ito et al., 2015).
source: However, when a rat repeatedly traverses the same location on its way to different destinations, the place fields of hippocampal place cells are strongly modulated by where the animal is going or where it has come from (Wood et al., 2000; Frank et al., 2000; Ferbinteanu and Shapiro, 2003; Bower et al., 2005; Ainge et al., 2007; Ji and Wilson, 2008; Pastalkova et al., 2008; Ferbinteanu et al., 2011; Allen et al., 2012; Catanese et al., 2014; Ito et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: Place cells represent not just near instantaneous location (Muller and Kubie, 1989), but also aspects of the animal's goal directed behaviour.
source: This suggests that place cells represent not just near instantaneous location (Muller and Kubie, 1989), but also aspects of the animal's goal directed behaviour.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature and the modulation findings.

claim: In a study by Ainge et al., 2007, rats ran up the central stem of a double-Y maze to gather reward in one of four goal boxes.
source: For example, in a study by Ainge et al., 2007, rats ran up the central stem of a double-Y maze to gather reward in one of four goal boxes.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of a cited study.

claim: Place fields on the central stem and on adjacent portions of the maze in the Ainge et al., 2007 study often exhibited strong modulation depending on the goal box the animal was headed towards (see Figure 3 in Ainge et al., 2007).
source: Place fields on the central stem and on adjacent portions of the maze often exhibited strong modulation depending on the goal box the animal was headed towards (see Figure 3 in Ainge et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes findings from a cited study.

claim: One interpretation of 'splitter cell' pattern of firing is that it represents the animal's intended destination.
source: One interpretation of this 'splitter cell' pattern of firing (hereafter differential firing) is that it represents the animal's intended destination.
evidence: This is one possible interpretation of the differential firing phenomenon.

claim: Another interpretation is that the prospective differential firing observed in the overlapping portions of the routes did not reflect the intended goal location per se, but rather the position along one of four separate trajectories.
source: However, another interpretation is possible. To reach each goal location, the rat traversed a partially overlapping, but distinct route. Each route was repeated multiple times until the reward was moved to a different goal box. It is possible that the prospective differential firing observed in the overlapping portions of the routes did not reflect the intended goal location per se, but rather the position along one of four separate trajectories.
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation proposed by the authors.

claim: The distinction between executing a series of responses and learning a goal location has a long tradition in spatial learning (Tolman et al., 1946; McCutchan, 1947; Restle, 1957).
source: This distinction between executing a series of responses and learning a goal location has a long tradition in spatial learning (Tolman et al., 1946; McCutchan, 1947; Restle, 1957).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the historical literature.

claim: If differential firing on the overlapping sections of different trajectories reflects the animal's intended destination, then firing on the overlapping sections of the two routes leading to the same goal should be similar.
source: If differential firing on the overlapping sections of different trajectories reflects the animal's intended destination, then firing on the overlapping sections of the two routes leading to the same goal should be similar (but should differ from firing on the routes leading to other goals).
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the goal-dependent hypothesis.

claim: If differential firing reflects position along a specific route, the firing on the two routes to the same goal should differ.
source: In contrast, if differential firing reflects position along a specific route, the firing on these two routes should differ (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the route-dependent hypothesis.

claim: The results support the route interpretation over the goal interpretation.
source: Our results support the latter interpretation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Place cells with fields on the overlapping portions of different routes leading to a common goal showed strong differential firing.
source: Place cells with fields on the overlapping portions of different routes leading to a common goal showed strong differential firing, and failed to show similar firing on different routes leading to the same goal.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Place cells failed to show similar firing on different routes leading to the same goal.
source: Place cells with fields on the overlapping portions of different routes leading to a common goal showed strong differential firing, and failed to show similar firing on different routes leading to the same goal.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Over the course of the first 10 sessions prior to surgery, the number of errors the animals made after the first correct trial in each block of trials decreased significantly over sessions (F(9,99) = 5.26, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.32).
source: Over the course of the first 10 sessions prior to surgery, the number of errors the animals made after the first correct trial in each block of trials decreased significantly over sessions (F(9,99) = 5.26, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.32; Figure 2A solid line).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral training data, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The time the rats took to complete each trial once they had located the rewarded goal in a block of trials decreased significantly across sessions (F(9,99) = 6.87, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.38).
source: The time the rats took to complete each trial once they had located the rewarded goal in a block of trials also decreased significantly across sessions (F(9,99) = 6.87, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.38; Figure 2B solid line).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral training data, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of errors per session on trials prior to finding the rewarded goal box in each block did not change significantly over sessions (F(9,99) = 1.80, p>0.05).
source: In contrast, neither the number of errors per session (F(9,99) = 1.80, p>0.05), nor the time per trial (F(9,99) = 1.95, p>0.05) on trials prior to finding the rewarded goal box in each block changed significantly over sessions (Figure 2A and B respectively, dashed lines).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral training data.

claim: The time per trial on trials prior to finding the rewarded goal box in each block did not change significantly over sessions (F(9,99) = 1.95, p>0.05).
source: In contrast, neither the number of errors per session (F(9,99) = 1.80, p>0.05), nor the time per trial (F(9,99) = 1.95, p>0.05) on trials prior to finding the rewarded goal box in each block changed significantly over sessions (Figure 2A and B respectively, dashed lines).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral training data.

claim: The rats could remember the last rewarded goal and learned to apply the win-stay, lose-shift rule.
source: Together, these results suggest that the rats could remember the last rewarded goal and learned to apply the win-stay, lose-shift rule, but that their efficiency in searching for the new goal location at the beginning of each block did not improve significantly across sessions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of behavioral results.

claim: The rats' efficiency in searching for the new goal location at the beginning of each block did not improve significantly across sessions.
source: Together, these results suggest that the rats could remember the last rewarded goal and learned to apply the win-stay, lose-shift rule, but that their efficiency in searching for the new goal location at the beginning of each block did not improve significantly across sessions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of behavioral results.

claim: Across all sessions, the rats averaged 9.08 s (S.D. = 6.19 s) to travel from the start box to the end of the maze on trials before they had identified the goal box which contained reward.
source: Across all sessions, the rats averaged 9.08 s (S.D. = 6.19 s) to travel from the start box to the end of the maze on trials before they had identified the goal box which contained reward.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the behavioral data.

claim: Once the rewarded goal box had been visited, travel time on later trials in that block decreased to 5.38 s (S.D. = 3.48 s).
source: Once the rewarded goal box had been visited, travel time on later trials in that block decreased to 5.38 s (S.D. = 3.48 s).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the behavioral data.

claim: During training the animals made a greater number of errors on the trials when Routes 2 or 3 to the Centre Goal Box were rewarded than on trials when the outer routes (Routes 1 or 4) to the Left and Right Goal Boxes, respectively, were rewarded (t(9) = 4.53, p<0.005, paired t-test).
source: During training the animals made a greater number of errors on the trials when Routes 2 or 3 to the Centre Goal Box were rewarded than on trials when the outer routes (Routes 1 or 4) to the Left and Right Goal Boxes, respectively, were rewarded (t(9) = 4.53, p<0.005, paired t-test, see Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Post-hoc multiple comparison tests confirmed Routes 2 and 3 were confused more than any other route pair (p<0.05 in all cases, with Sidak correction).
source: Post-hoc multiple comparison tests confirmed Routes 2 and 3 were confused more than any other route pair (p<0.05 in all cases, with Sidak correction).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc tests on the behavioral data.

claim: In total, 377 place cells that were active on the maze were recorded from eight rats.
source: In total, we recorded 377 place cells that were active on the maze from eight rats.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the recorded data.

claim: Place cells were more likely to have a place field in the initial areas of the maze (e.g., the start box, central stem and first choice point) than in later ones.
source: Place cells were more likely to have a place field in the initial areas of the maze (e.g., the start box, central stem and first choice point) than in later ones (Figure 3A; see also Ainge et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of place cell distribution, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a significant negative correlation between distance of the sector from the start box and the number of recorded place cells that were active in that sector (r(12) = -0.78, p<0.05).
source: Consistent with this, there was a significant negative correlation between distance of the sector from the start box and the number of recorded place cells that were active in that sector (r(12) = -0.78, p<0.05; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of place cell distribution, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Neither running speed, nor cell firing rate showed a direct relationship with distance from the start box.
source: Neither running speed, nor cell firing rate showed such a direct relationship with distance from the start box (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 284 place cells were assessed by rANCOVA in at least one of the four sectors that were analysed for route/goal-dependent activity.
source: In the maze environment, 284 place cells were assessed by rANCOVA in at least one of the four sectors that were analysed for route/goal-dependent activity (Figure 1C; start box, central stem, left stem and right stem).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the analysis.

claim: Of the 284 assessed place cells, 161 cells (57%) showed differential firing in at least one sector based on the rANCOVA results.
source: Of these, 161 cells (57%) showed differential firing in at least one sector based on the rANCOVA results.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: 83/176 assessed cells (47%) showed significantly different firing rates in the start box between the four trajectories.
source: Examining each of the four sectors of the maze separately, 83/176 assessed cells (47%) showed significantly different firing rates in the start box between the four trajectories (termed differential firing; see Video 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis, with reference to Video 1.

claim: 61/158 (43%) cells showed differential firing in the central stem.
source: 61/158 (43%) cells showed differential firing in the central stem, and 16/124 (13%) and 14/115 (12%) showed differential firing in the left and right stems respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 16/124 (13%) cells showed differential firing in the left stem.
source: 61/158 (43%) cells showed differential firing in the central stem, and 16/124 (13%) and 14/115 (12%) showed differential firing in the left and right stems respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 14/115 (12%) cells showed differential firing in the right stem.
source: 61/158 (43%) cells showed differential firing in the central stem, and 16/124 (13%) and 14/115 (12%) showed differential firing in the left and right stems respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In the start box, differential firing did not reflect anticipatory firing before the holding block was removed.
source: In the start box, differential firing did not reflect anticipatory firing before the holding block was removed, as cells with differential firing did not differ from other active place cells (Figure 3F; (F(1,257) = 0.25, p>0.80, ηp2<0.10, tested by repeated measures ANOVA looking at firing rate x time bin (four equally spaced intervals) x cell type).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis, shown in Figure 3F.

claim: 48 cells were identified with differential firing patterns where they fired significantly differently on one route compared to the other three, or fired similarly on Routes 2 and 3 but differently from Routes 1 and 4.
source: Overall, 48 cells were identified with one of these patterns of activity, and of these, 9 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 1 than on the other 3 routes, 13 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 2, 18 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 3, and 6 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 4.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the post-hoc analysis.

claim: 9 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 1 than on the other 3 routes.
source: Overall, 48 cells were identified with one of these patterns of activity, and of these, 9 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 1 than on the other 3 routes, 13 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 2, 18 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 3, and 6 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 4.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the post-hoc analysis.

claim: 13 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 2.
source: Overall, 48 cells were identified with one of these patterns of activity, and of these, 9 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 1 than on the other 3 routes, 13 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 2, 18 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 3, and 6 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 4.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the post-hoc analysis.

claim: 18 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 3.
source: Overall, 48 cells were identified with one of these patterns of activity, and of these, 9 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 1 than on the other 3 routes, 13 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 2, 18 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 3, and 6 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 4.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the post-hoc analysis.

claim: 6 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 4.
source: Overall, 48 cells were identified with one of these patterns of activity, and of these, 9 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 1 than on the other 3 routes, 13 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 2, 18 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 3, and 6 cells fired at a significantly different rate on Route 4.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the post-hoc analysis.

claim: Only two cells fired similarly and at a significantly higher rate for Routes 2 and 3 than for Routes 1 and 4.
source: Only two cells fired similarly and at a significantly higher rate for Routes 2 and 3 than for Routes 1 and 4.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the post-hoc analysis.

claim: The probability of observing the pattern where only two cells showed goal-dependent firing by chance is low (X2(4, N = 48) = 15.96, p<0.004, Fischer's exact test).
source: The probability of observing this pattern by chance is low (X2(4, N = 48) = 15.96, p<0.004, Fischer's exact test, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For the majority (95.8%) of place cells which fired significantly differently on at least one of the routes to the Centre Goal Box, firing appeared to be related to the specific intended route.
source: First, for the majority (95.8%) of place cells which fired significantly differently on at least one of the routes to the Centre Goal Box, firing appeared to be related to the specific intended route.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the analysis.

claim: In only two (4.2%) of the cells did the firing rate appear to be related to the intended goal, independent of the route.
source: In only two (4.2%) of the cells did the firing rate appear to be related to the intended goal, independent of the route.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the analysis.

claim: The pattern of results is significantly different than expected if equal numbers of cells had coded Route 2, Route 3 and both routes (X2(1, N = 33) = 25.49, p<0.0001, Fischer's exact test).
source: This pattern of results is significantly different than expected if equal numbers of cells had coded Route 2, Route 3 and both routes (X2(1, N = 33) = 25.49, p<0.0001, Fischer's exact test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: 69% (33/48) of the cells included in the analysis fired preferentially on one (or both) routes to the Centre Goal Box (Routes 2 or 3).
source: Second, of the cells included in this analysis, 69% (33/48) fired preferentially on one (or both) routes to the Centre Goal Box (Routes 2 or 3), whereas only 31% (15/48) fired preferentially on one of the routes to the outer goals (Routes 1 or 4).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the analysis.

claim: Only 31% (15/48) of the cells fired preferentially on one of the routes to the outer goals (Routes 1 or 4).
source: Second, of the cells included in this analysis, 69% (33/48) fired preferentially on one (or both) routes to the Centre Goal Box (Routes 2 or 3), whereas only 31% (15/48) fired preferentially on one of the routes to the outer goals (Routes 1 or 4).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the analysis.

claim: The probability of observing the pattern of more route coding for the two routes to the Centre Goal Box than to the two routes to the outer goal boxes by chance is low (X2(1, N = 48) = 6.75, p<0.015, Fischer's exact test).
source: The probability of observing this pattern of results by chance is also low (X2(1, N = 48) = 6.75, p<0.015, Fischer's exact test), and indicates significantly more route coding for the two routes to the Centre Goal Box than to the two routes to the outer goal boxes.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: In the segments of the maze just after the first choice point, 30 cells (16 or 12.9% in the left stem, 14 or 12.2% in the right stem) were found to fire significantly differently depending on the trajectory of the animal.
source: In the segments of the maze just after the first choice point, 30 cells (16 or 12.9% in the left stem, 14 or 12.2% in the right stem) were found to fire significantly differently depending on the trajectory of the animal.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the analysis.

claim: Over-representation of Routes 2 and 3 in the left and right stems is not statistically significant (X2(1, N = 30) = 0.53, p>0.5, Fischer's exact test).
source: Over-representation of Routes 2 and 3 also appeared to be present here, however this effect is not statistically significant (X2(1, N = 30) = 0.53, p>0.5, Fischer's exact test; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Place cells with significant differential activity on the maze did not differ from place cells without such activity in terms of isolation distances (D = 0.10, p>0.90).
source: Place cells with significant differential activity on the maze did not differ from place cells without such activity in terms of isolation distances (D = 0.10, p>0.90), distribution of Lratios (D = 0.25, p>0.40), signal-to-noise ratios (D = 0.2, p>0.70), or peak waveform amplitude (D = 0.2, p>0.70) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cluster quality analysis, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Place cells with significant differential activity on the maze did not differ from place cells without such activity in terms of distribution of Lratios (D = 0.25, p>0.40).
source: Place cells with significant differential activity on the maze did not differ from place cells without such activity in terms of isolation distances (D = 0.10, p>0.90), distribution of Lratios (D = 0.25, p>0.40), signal-to-noise ratios (D = 0.2, p>0.70), or peak waveform amplitude (D = 0.2, p>0.70) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cluster quality analysis, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Place cells with significant differential activity on the maze did not differ from place cells without such activity in terms of signal-to-noise ratios (D = 0.2, p>0.70).
source: Place cells with significant differential activity on the maze did not differ from place cells without such activity in terms of isolation distances (D = 0.10, p>0.90), distribution of Lratios (D = 0.25, p>0.40), signal-to-noise ratios (D = 0.2, p>0.70), or peak waveform amplitude (D = 0.2, p>0.70) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cluster quality analysis, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Place cells with significant differential activity on the maze did not differ from place cells without such activity in terms of peak waveform amplitude (D = 0.2, p>0.70).
source: Place cells with significant differential activity on the maze did not differ from place cells without such activity in terms of isolation distances (D = 0.10, p>0.90), distribution of Lratios (D = 0.25, p>0.40), signal-to-noise ratios (D = 0.2, p>0.70), or peak waveform amplitude (D = 0.2, p>0.70) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cluster quality analysis, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: No relationship was detected between isolation distance and rANCOVA F-statistic (r(573) = 0.05, p>0.20).
source: Nor did we detect any relationship between these four measures and rANCOVA F-statistic (r(573) = 0.05, p>0.20, r(573) = −0.08, p>0.05, r(573) = 0.03, p>0.40 and r(573) = 0.01, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis.

claim: No relationship was detected between Lratio and rANCOVA F-statistic (r(573) = −0.08, p>0.05).
source: Nor did we detect any relationship between these four measures and rANCOVA F-statistic (r(573) = 0.05, p>0.20, r(573) = −0.08, p>0.05, r(573) = 0.03, p>0.40 and r(573) = 0.01, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis.

claim: No relationship was detected between signal-to-noise ratio and rANCOVA F-statistic (r(573) = 0.03, p>0.40).
source: Nor did we detect any relationship between these four measures and rANCOVA F-statistic (r(573) = 0.05, p>0.20, r(573) = −0.08, p>0.05, r(573) = 0.03, p>0.40 and r(573) = 0.01, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis.

claim: No relationship was detected between peak waveform amplitude and rANCOVA F-statistic (r(573) = 0.01, p>0.05).
source: Nor did we detect any relationship between these four measures and rANCOVA F-statistic (r(573) = 0.05, p>0.20, r(573) = −0.08, p>0.05, r(573) = 0.03, p>0.40 and r(573) = 0.01, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis.

claim: 25 ensembles from six rats with an average of 11.12 cells/ensemble (SD = 5.67) were analyzed.
source: To test the accuracy with which an animal's trajectory could be identified based on the average firing rate of place cell ensembles we analysed 25 ensembles from six rats with an average of 11.12 cells/ensemble (SD = 5.67).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the ensemble analysis.

claim: Ensembles had to contain at least six place cells, and the largest ensemble contained 27 cells.
source: Ensembles had to contain at least six place cells, and the largest ensemble contained 27 cells.
evidence: This describes the criteria and range for the ensemble analysis.

claim: At the ensemble level, population vectors representing trajectories along Routes 1–4 in the start box and central stem were consistently matched to their correct goal population vector at a rate greater than incorrect goal population vectors.
source: At the ensemble level, population vectors representing trajectories along Routes 1–4 in the start box and central stem were consistently matched to their correct goal population vector at a rate greater than incorrect goal population vectors (Figure 7A - start box, and 7E - central stem).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, shown in Figures 7A and 7E.

claim: These matches were made at an above chance level, regardless of the final goal destination (p<10–3 in all cases).
source: These matches were made at an above chance level, regardless of the final goal destination (p<10–3 in all cases, Figure 7D and F respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ensemble analysis, shown in Figures 7D and 7F.

claim: Population vectors representing trajectories on the central two routes leading to the same goal were not matched to the alternative central route at an above chance level (p>0.9 in all cases).
source: Furthermore, population vectors representing trajectories on the central two routes leading to the same goal were not matched to the alternative central route at an above chance level (p>0.9 in all cases).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ensemble analysis.

claim: At the ensemble level, place cell firing patterns were not dependent on the final goal destination but on the immediate trajectory.
source: These results confirm that at the ensemble level, as with the single cell level, place cell firing patterns were not dependent on the final goal destination but on the immediate trajectory.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ensemble analysis results.

claim: Ensemble information alone was sufficient to decode the animal's future destination at an above chance level.
source: Furthermore, this information alone was sufficient to decode the animal's future destination at an above chance level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ensemble analysis results.

claim: There was no relationship between the position of a trial within a block and the likelihood of this trajectory being correctly matched to its goal population vector (p>0.05).
source: Also, there was no relationship between the position of a trial within a block and the likelihood of this trajectory being correctly matched to its goal population vector or the cosine similarity value resulting from this comparison (p>0.05 in both cases) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) suggesting that this trajectory coding persisted throughout blocks of trials.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ensemble analysis, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no relationship between the position of a trial within a block and the cosine similarity value resulting from the comparison (p>0.05).
source: Also, there was no relationship between the position of a trial within a block and the likelihood of this trajectory being correctly matched to its goal population vector or the cosine similarity value resulting from this comparison (p>0.05 in both cases) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) suggesting that this trajectory coding persisted throughout blocks of trials.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ensemble analysis, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.
